clinicalPearls: Characterised by fixed, symmetrical, well-demarcated erythematous hyperkeratotic plaques, typically over the extensor limbs, buttocks and face
Lesions are relatively stable in position (unlike the migratory figures of erythrokeratodermia variabilis) but slowly progress, often during childhood
A palmoplantar keratoderma is present in many affected individuals
Inheritance is usually autosomal dominant, and it shows genetic overlap with erythrokeratodermia variabilis, with variants reported in connexin and other keratinisation genes such as KRT83 and LOR
There is considerable clinical and genetic overlap with erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva, and the two are often considered a spectrum
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by biopsy showing hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and papillomatosis; molecular testing may identify a causative variant
Management is supportive with emollients and keratolytics, and oral retinoids can substantially improve the hyperkeratosis in severe disease
reference.pathophysiology: Progressive symmetric erythrokeratodermia is a genetically heterogeneous disorder of keratinisation. Reported causes include variants affecting gap-junction connexins, loricrin and hair-keratin genes such as KRT83, which disturb keratinocyte communication, cornified-envelope formation and terminal differentiation. The result is a chronic disturbance of epidermal proliferation and differentiation, generating persistent symmetric erythematous hyperkeratotic plaques with a background of increased epidermal turnover, and a frequently associated palmoplantar keratoderma. Its overlap with erythrokeratodermia variabilis reflects shared molecular pathways.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and papillomatosis
Molecular genetic testing of connexin, LOR and keratin genes as indicated
Clinical photography to document progression and symmetry
Exclusion of psoriasis and pityriasis rubra pilaris where clinically uncertain
redFlags: Rapid extension or erythroderma with barrier compromise
Deep painful fissuring of associated palmoplantar keratoderma
Atypical features prompting reconsideration of an inflammatory or syndromic diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The condition is chronic and tends to progress through childhood before stabilising; it is not life-threatening, and many patients respond well to oral retinoids, though relapse on withdrawal is common.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the fixed plaques as psoriasis or pityriasis rubra pilaris
Failing to recognise the overlap with erythrokeratodermia variabilis
Stopping effective retinoid therapy abruptly with subsequent relapse
management: Oral retinoids such as acitretin as the mainstay for extensive hyperkeratotic disease, normalising the disturbed keratinisation
Topical keratolytics including urea, salicylic acid and lactic acid, combined with regular emollients to reduce scale
Topical retinoids or vitamin D analogues for localised plaques
Dedicated care of associated palmoplantar keratoderma to preserve hand and foot function
Genetic counselling and family screening given the usually autosomal dominant inheritance and reported connexin, loricrin and keratin gene variants
Monitoring for relapse on retinoid withdrawal and surveillance for retinoid-related adverse effects
Coordinated dermatology and clinical genetics follow-up to document progression and guide therapy
